cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-lazarus-en.summary: In the upper register Christ calls Lazarus, still wrapped in his grave-clothes, from the tomb while Mary and Martha kneel; beside it Christ reclines at table as a woman anoints his feet. Below, Christ rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, followed by the apostles, as children and townspeople come out of the city gate to greet him.
facts: Wikipedia singles out the Raising of Lazarus among the manuscript's biblical images.

The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-lazarus-en.notes: Folio derived from the Gallica image sequence (view number minus 13, halved) and checked against folios named on other Commons files of this manuscript; the Commons file name gives the Gallica view number, not the folio.

cur:manuscripts-valcavado-son-of-man.summary: Beneath seven burning lamps, the Son of Man sits on a throne with a sword issuing from his mouth and stars at his side, while John, fallen at his feet, is raised by his hand and an angel stands at the right; below, John, labelled, writes his book beside the seven churches drawn as arcades with their names.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.
cur:manuscripts-valcavado-son-of-man.notes: The upper scene is somewhat worn; description based on the visible figures and the usual Beatus iconography of this passage.

Q2667782.summary: In the central panel of this great triptych, Christ's pale body slides down a white winding-sheet into the arms of his friends, caught by John in red while Mary Magdalene steadies his foot. The wings show the Visitation and the Presentation in the Temple, so that every panel shows someone carrying Christ. It is one of the most celebrated altarpieces of the Baroque and the companion of Rubens's Elevation of the Cross in the same cathedral.
facts: It was commissioned in 1611 by the Arquebusiers' Guild, whose patron saint was Saint Christopher (literally 'Christ-bearer'); the theme of bearing Christ unites all three panels, and Christopher himself appears on the outer wings.
The Antwerp triptychs inspired the climax of Ouida's 1872 novel A Dog of Flanders, whose young hero Nello dies before Rubens's paintings in the cathedral.
Like the Elevation, it was taken to Paris by the French in 1794 and returned to Antwerp in 1815.

Q3543898.summary: Against a dark, empty ground, Goya's Christ hangs serene and luminous, his gaze lifted heavenward, his body modelled with a smooth, idealized classicism. Painted as the young artist's reception piece for the Royal Academy of San Fernando, it shows Goya mastering the academic language of his day before he went on to transform Spanish art.
facts: Goya presented it to the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando in May 1780, and with it he was admitted as an académico de mérito (academician of merit).
The composition echoes Velázquez's famous Christ Crucified, borrowing its dark, empty background, and the Neoclassicism of Anton Raphael Mengs, whose taste then dominated the Academy.
Following Spanish tradition codified by Francisco Pacheco, Christ is fixed with four nails and rests his feet on a small wooden support (suppedaneum).
In 1785 the painting was sent to the Franciscan church of San Francisco el Grande in Madrid, whose decoration was promoted by King Charles III; it later passed to the Prado.
